The biggest issue of Roe v Wade is that it has no business being decided at the federal level. The written opinion is also very poorly reasoned, and the arguments used are contradicted by various other SCOTUS opinions(including National Federation of Independent Business et al. v. Sebelius).

Just because something is good doesn't mean that the federal government ought to mandate its legalization. Just because something is bad doesn't mean the federal government ought to mandate its prohibition. For example, the federal government does not involve itself in criminalizing murder; each individual state does.

The USA is composed of states for many reasons. One of these reasons is so that people can "agree to disagree" on divisive and controversial issues and different states can have different policies regarding the legalization or regulation of such issues.

I agree to a point, but on the other side - what keeps America as a world leader is the fact that we are united at a federal level (much more so than the European union or any other governing body). While I do support state soverignty there are some decisions that should be decided at the federal level. I do hold many conservative values but at some level (such as interstate commerce) it just makes sense to have a governing body say that free markets among states is the decision. Driver's licenses are completely universal among states (I wish that concealed carry laws also applied) some things (basic services) need to be decided at the federal level - then states can impose individual regulations.

I think that a lot of our success can be attributed to the fact that the USA is a combination of fifty individual nations joined together for common goals. I think our status as a "world leader," however much it may depend a strong centralized government, probably brings us more costs than it does benefits.

Of course some things ought to be decided at the federal level, but at this point we have progressed far beyond those subjects.

Our constitution was written with very strictly prescribed federal powers and duties. Facilitating commerce between multiple states, a valid and constitutional power, has been twisted so far beyond its intended scope that it can now justify any federal action. Wickard v. Filburn is the easiest example, where "interstate commerce" was determined to include a farmer growing wheat on his own land to feed to his own livestock.
